segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since Christ, then, suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same way of thinking, because whoever has suffered in the flesh has finished with sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so as to live the rest of your time in the flesh no longer by human desires but by the will of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the time already past was enough for doing what the Gentiles choose to do, living in debauchery, desires, drunkenness, revels, drinking parties, and forbidden idolatries.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They think it strange now that you do not rush with them into the same flood of reckless living, and so they slander you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they will give an account to the one who stands ready to judge the living and the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is why the good news was announced to the dead as well: so that, though judged in the flesh by human standards, they might live in the spirit by God's standard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The end of all things has come near. So keep a sound mind and stay sober for the sake of your prayers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Above all, keep your love for one another constant, because love covers a multitude of sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As each of you has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of the varied grace of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone speaks, let it be as one speaking God's own words; if anyone serves, as one serving by the strength that God supplies, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Dear friends, do not think it strange that a fiery ordeal has come among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rather, to the degree that you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may also rejoice and exult.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or a wrongdoer, or as a meddler in other people's affairs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone suffers as a Christian, they should not be ashamed, but should glorify God in this name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the time has come for judgment to begin with the house of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who disobey the good news of God?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “if the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let those who suffer according to the will of God entrust their lives to a faithful Creator as they do good.

notes.phrase: whoever has suffered in the flesh has finished with sin
notes.traditional: he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin
notes.note: The clause is compact and disputed. It may describe the believer who, by accepting suffering, has made a decisive break with sin; it may refer to Christ himself; or it may echo the idea that one who has died with Christ in baptism is freed from sin. The opening word can also mean ‘that’ instead of ‘because’, making the clause the content of the ‘way of thinking’. The rendering leaves these options open as far as English allows.

The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’ and, in the plural, was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses both ‘Gentiles’ and ‘nations’ for this one word. The readers of this letter appear to have been largely non-Jews themselves, so the term here marks the pagan society they have left, not their ancestry.

Most current scholars take ‘the dead’ to be believers who heard the good news while alive and have since died: condemned in human eyes, they will nevertheless live before God. Others connect the verse with 3:19 and understand a proclamation to the dead in the underworld, and an older view takes ‘dead’ to mean spiritually dead. The Greek does not settle the question, and ‘in the spirit’ could also be read as ‘by the Spirit’.

notes.phrase: love covers a multitude of sins
notes.note: This echoes Proverbs 10:12 in a form closer to the Hebrew text than to the Greek Septuagint, and the same saying appears in James 5:20. It seems to have circulated as a proverb among early Christians. Whether the sins covered are those of the one loved or of the one who loves is not stated.

The Greek word denotes a saying of divine origin and is used in the Septuagint for words spoken by God. ‘Oracles’ is the traditional rendering and is accurate, but it suggests pagan shrines to many modern readers. The point is that anyone who speaks in the community should do so as one delivering what comes from God.

The word means a burning and was used of the smelting furnace in which metal is refined and proved genuine. The letter has already used this picture in 1:7, where faith is tested like gold in fire. The suffering is thus presented as a test that proves, not as mere destruction.

notes.phrase: the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you
notes.traditional: the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified
notes.note: Later manuscripts add a sentence at the end of this verse (‘on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified’), which is why it appears in the King James Version. Some manuscripts also read ‘the Spirit of glory and of power and of God’. The edition translated here, with most modern editions, regards both as additions. The wording echoes Isaiah 11:2.

notes.phrase: a meddler in other people's affairs
notes.traditional: a busybody in other men's matters
notes.note: This word is not found in any earlier Greek text and may have been coined by the author; it combines ‘belonging to another’ with ‘overseer’. Most scholars take it to mean someone who interferes in matters that are not their concern. Other proposals include an embezzler of property held in trust or a political agitator. The meaning remains uncertain.

The word occurs only three times in the New Testament (also Acts 11:26 and 26:28). It is formed in the Latin manner to mean a partisan or adherent of Christ. It was probably coined by outsiders, perhaps as a term of contempt. Here it appears as a label under which believers may be accused, and the letter tells them to bear it as an honour.

The Greek word means both a building and a household. It may refer to the community as God's household, or, following 2:5 where believers are a ‘spiritual house’, as God's temple. The idea of judgment beginning at God's sanctuary echoes Ezekiel 9:6. ‘House’ is kept because it can carry either sense.

notes.phrase: “if the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”
notes.note: This quotes Proverbs 11:31 almost word for word in its Greek (Septuagint) form. That form differs from the Hebrew, which speaks of the righteous being repaid on earth. ‘Barely’ means ‘with difficulty’: it does not cast doubt on the outcome but points to the hardship through which the righteous are brought.

The Greek word covers a person's life and self as well as the inner person, and with a verb of entrusting it means handing oneself over for safekeeping. ‘Souls’ is the traditional rendering, but it may suggest to a modern reader an immaterial part distinct from the person. Many modern translations render ‘entrust themselves’.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the New Testament in senses from bodily life to sinful nature, and translations vary widely between ‘flesh’, ‘body’, ‘human nature’ and ‘earthly life’.
The verb and its noun εὐαγγέλιον (v. 17) need one decision between ‘gospel’ / ‘preach the gospel’ and ‘good news’ / ‘announce the good news’ across all books.
The choice between ‘soul’, ‘life’ and ‘self’ recurs throughout the New Testament and shapes how readers understand human nature in these texts.
The word means both testing and temptation, and the choice between ‘trial’, ‘test’ and ‘temptation’ should be governed consistently by sense.
It is used of abusive speech against people as well as against God, and readers are misled if ‘blaspheme’, ‘slander’ and ‘revile’ alternate without a rule.
